headline: Highest risk is capability conflict: both CLIs can write the same filesystem and run shells, while Gemini CLI also uses MCP and broad network egress.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can use MCP and reads/writes repo files; slim reads/writes filesystem artifacts and runs shell commands. If Gemini ingests slim-produced files or command output as instructions, a shared filesystem bridge exists. No clipboard or direct message channel is documented, so this is not high.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI is configured to consume slim-generated files as prompts or instructions, injection becomes plausible.
IF both agents operate in the same working directory, file-based prompt injection is reachable.
mitigations: Separate working directories for the two agents.
Disable automatic ingestion of files produced by the other agent.
Review any MCP server outputs before reuse.
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files in cwd and have broad network egress. Gemini CLI handles source code, shell environment, and optional API credentials; slim handles filesystem artifacts, environment variables, and registry credentials. A shared workspace can leak sensitive files from one agent into the other’s outputs or network calls.
conditions: IF the agents share a writable workspace, files touched by one can be read by the other.
IF either agent is pointed at secrets-bearing directories, those secrets can be exposed through logs or network requests.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent.
Exclude secrets directories from both agents.
Rotate any credentials present in shared paths.
Run both agents with least-privilege environment variables.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shells and write the filesystem; Gemini CLI also modifies git state, while slim can run subprocesses in a temporary container. In a shared repo, concurrent writes and git mutations can race or overwrite each other. The profiles do not show locking, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, conflicting writes are possible.
IF Gemini CLI commits or rewrites files while slim is generating artifacts, state corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate branches or clones.
Serialize write operations manually.
Pause one agent before the other edits the repo.
Use git worktrees for isolation.
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared mutable paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can produce shell and file outputs that slim may consume during image analysis or container manipulation. slim’s interactive command execution can then act on those outputs without a documented verification gate. That creates a plausible A-to-B error cascade, though not an automatic one.
conditions: IF slim is fed Gemini-generated commands or Dockerfile edits without review, errors can propagate.
IF Gemini fabricates file contents that slim later executes or packages, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human review before slim executes generated commands.
Compare generated artifacts against source inputs.
Use dry-run mode where available.
Keep Gemini outputs as suggestions only.
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Gemini CLI may handle Google account login and GEMINI_API_KEY, while slim handles registry credentials and certificate private keys. If both are used on the same sensitive workspace, differing retention and logging practices can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not document a shared certification boundary, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated secrets such as private keys or registry credentials are present in the shared workspace, compliance exposure increases.
IF either agent logs or uploads those secrets, retention and residency obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated secrets out of shared directories.
Review logging settings for both tools.
Use separate service accounts and credentials.
Document data-handling boundaries for each agent.
requires-engineering: map each data class to an approved residency and retention policy.
